t: LeetCode 1521 — Find a Value of a Mysterious Function Closest to Target
o: Decoding the picture, func(arr, l, r) is the bitwise AND of arr[l..r], and we must minimize |func(arr, l, r) - target| over all windows. In example 1 (arr = [9,12,3,7,15], target = 5) the fifteen window values are 9,12,3,7,15,8,0,3,7,0,0,3,0,0,0; the closest to 5 are 3 and 7, giving 2. AND only clears bits as a window grows, so for a FIXED right endpoint the subarrays ending there produce at most one distinct value per bit of the maximum element — roughly 20 values for arr[i] <= 10^6. That collapse of exponentially many windows into a logarithmic list is the heart of the optimal solution.
k: AND is monotone shrinking: widening a window can only turn bits off, never on.
Subarrays ending at index r have at most log2(max(arr)) + 1 distinct AND values, enabling an O(n log C) sweep.
Every achievable window AND shows up in some per-r list, so examining those lists covers the entire search space.

a.i: Fix the left endpoint and extend the right one, maintaining the running AND incrementally instead of recomputing each window from scratch. Straightforward and correct, but quadratic — hopeless at n = 10^5 unless data happens to allow early exits.
s: For each left index l initialize cur to the all-ones mask.
Extend r from l to the end, updating cur &= arr[r].
Track the minimum of |cur - target| across all windows.
a.t: O(n^2) — every one of the n(n+1)/2 windows is touched in the worst case.
a.sp: O(1) — a running AND and the best answer.

a.n: Approach 2: Distinct AND Values per Right Endpoint
a.i: Keep vals, the strictly-decreasing distinct ANDs of all subarrays ending at the previous element (shortest window first, hence largest value first). When the new element x arrives, the fresh candidate set is x followed by v & x for each prior v — still non-increasing, so adjacent dedup keeps it minimal, and its length never exceeds the bit width (~20 for 10^6). Update the answer with every candidate and roll the list forward; nothing outside these lists can ever be achieved.
s: Initialize vals as empty and ans to infinity.
For each x rebuild: nxt = [x], then append v & x for each v in vals whenever it differs from the last appended value.
Update ans with |w - target| for every w in nxt.
Replace vals with nxt and continue; return ans at the end.
a.t: O(n * B) where B ~ 20 is the bit length of max(arr) — each step rebuilds a list capped at B+1 strictly decreasing values.
a.sp: O(B) — the candidate list for the current right endpoint.

w: Identifying func as AND is step one; the real test is spotting that per-right-endpoint AND values collapse to at most ~20 distinct results. Pitfalls: reading the function as OR, dropping single-element windows (seeding with x handles them), and trying sliding-window heuristics — AND is not invertible, so standard two-pointer tricks fail. Edge cases: all-equal arrays (list stays length 1), target above every achievable AND, n = 1. Follow-ups: the same few-distinct-values trick solves OR and GCD window problems, and a Sparse-table/binary-search variant finds the nearest value above or below target specifically.
